problem: Learned visual navigation controllers (CNN, multi-frame CNN, CNN+LSTM) fail in real, diverse environments because local sensing is partially observable (limited FOV, moving obstacles, hidden task progress) and behavior must be multimodal given a global objective; naive composition of CNN, memory and MDN ideas does not handle these together.
motivation: Robots need to navigate indoors and outdoors with vision only and compose behaviors like turning, obstacle avoidance and elevator riding. Reactive or shallow-memory policies cannot infer hidden state (e.g. an obstacle in the camera blind spot, or which floor the robot is on), and a single memory collapses different behavior modes to an averaged unimodal policy.
key_idea: Insert ConvLSTM memory layers at multiple depths of a CNN (multi-scale temporal modeling) with separate memory cells per behavior mode (multimodal memory) selected by a high-level mode signal, trained end-to-end by imitation.
insight: Memory at a single level (early or late) gives little benefit, while memory at multiple scales gives large gains: on blind-spot avoidance the late-only variant gets 10% SR and the full model 90%. Elevator riding SR goes from 0 (CNN+LSTM) to 90 with multi-scale memory, so memory placement matters, not just having a history. Separating memory per mode prevents mode collapse: without it the robot always drives straight (0% vs 90% SR on loop closure), and t-SNE shows features separable by mode only with the separate memories.
method: Memory module: modified ConvLSTM (peephole) with GroupNorm (G=32) after each conv for stable gradients and small-batch deployment, plus channel-wise recurrent dropout and Monte Carlo dropout to avoid overfitting to temporal redundancy
Multi-scale temporal modeling: three memory layers inserted at different depths of a CNN so history is fused at both low-level (motion, edges) and high-level (semantic) feature scales

Multimodal memory: each memory layer has one independent memory cell per mode (forward, left, right, elevator); a symbolic mode signal from the high-level planner selects which cell propagates features
Imitation learning: L2 loss on (steering, velocity) from teleoperated demonstrations (410K steps, 7.6 h, part collected with HG-DAgger for elevator), dataset resampling to balance modes
Training: TBPTT with sequences L=35 on every third frame, AdamW, 112x112 input, color jitter, 200 epochs (40 h on 4 RTX2080Ti)
Integration: plugged into the Intention-Net framework, where global planning on a crude map gives the mode signal to the local controller

setting.backbone: Small custom CNN with 3 ConvLSTM memory layers and MLP head (trained from scratch, imitation learning)
setting.training_data: 410K time steps (7.6 h) of human teleoperation demonstrations on Spot, including 64K HG-DAgger steps for elevator riding; no data collected for pedestrian and blind-spot tasks
setting.observation: monocular RGB (RealSense D435i) resized to 112x112, plus discrete mode signal
setting.privileged: none (mode signal from high-level planner on a crude map)

numbers.evidence: Table I: performance under partial observability (N=10)

numbers.eval_set_note: N=10 trials, 4 steps, tested at night

numbers.backbone: 3-layer CNN + 3 multi-scale ConvLSTM layers with per-mode memory
numbers.evidence: Table II: navigation with multimodal policy (N=10)

numbers_note: Method name is a macro in the source and not printed; described generically. Only small real-robot trials (N=10); no standard benchmarks.
results: The full controller reaches 90% SR on pedestrian avoidance, blind-spot avoidance and elevator riding, near the human operator (90/90/100), while CNN, multi-frame CNN and CNN+LSTM baselines get 0-30% SR (CNN+LSTM CR 90.1/88/83). Removing per-mode memory drops loop-closure SR from 90% to 0%.
limitations: Small-scale real-world evaluation (N=10 trials per task), hand-designed tasks, no standard benchmark
Depends on a discrete mode signal from a high-level planner and limited real-world demonstration data
Unclear whether the architecture can handle complex long-horizon interactive behaviors such as crowd navigation
